articles.title: US to keep 50,000 troops in Middle East amid Iran war, deployment may extend to 2027: Report
articles.summary: International News: The United States is planning to extend its troop deployment in West Asia to 2027 amid the Iran conflict escalating in its seventh month. The extended.
articles.body: The United States is planning to extend its troop deployment in West Asia to 2027 amid the Iran conflict escalating in its seventh month. The extended deployment could include the US Army’s 82nd airborne division, according to a letter sent to the families of deployed troops, read by The Wall Street Journal.The development comes after the United States Central Command (Centcom) carried out strikes on multiple sites inside Iran on Tuesday. Centcom confirmed the attacks on Wednesday, while Tehran responded with strikes on US-linked facilities across the Gulf. Iranian officials said the latest US strikes killed 18 people and wounded 142 others.According to The Wall Street Journal, the Pentagon is maintaining a major military presence in the region to preserve Trump’s options as he decides the next course of the war. The US has around 50,000 troops in the region, while 19 warships, air-defence units, fighter squadrons and paratroopers have been deployed.US forces are currently tasked with intercepting Iranian missiles, protecting commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz and blockading Iranian ports and coastal areas. The military is also prepared for larger offensive operations if Trump decides to escalate.The WSJ reported that Trump received briefings last month on options including intensified airstrikes, deploying ground troops to seize Iranian islands near Hormuz and bombing Pickaxe Mountain, a fortified site that could be used for covert nuclear activity.Extended deployment strains US troopsThe prolonged conflict is putting pressure on US service members and their families while contributing to maintenance delays that could take years to resolve, according to the WSJ.Army air-defence units have seen their usual deployment period increase from nine months to 12 months. Some units shifted from planned positions in Europe and the Pacific have already spent more than a year in the Middle East.The US Navy also has 19 warships in the region, including two aircraft carriers and 13 guided-missile destroyers. Several destroyers are now remaining at sea for months at a time rather than taking regular breaks, the WSJ reported.Trump has increasingly relied on economic pressure, hoping it will compel Tehran to negotiate. Last week, the US launched Operation Economic Outcast, targeting Iran’s major economic pillars, including oil, shipping, aviation and digital assets, according to ANI.Trump believes continued economic pressure could eventually push Iran to dismantle its nuclear programme or lead to the regime’s collapse.“I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing,” he wrote on social media. “They are just playing out the inevitable. When are the Iranian people going to rise up and fight?”However, Tehran has shown no indication of backing down, with the US and Iran continuing to exchange fire as both sides assert control over the Strait of Hormuz.As the latest confrontation unfolded, US forces also struck nearly 60 Iranian military sites around the strait, targeting air-defence systems, radar installations, maritime infrastructure, mine-laying facilities and communications networks. The US guided 40 commercial vessels through the waterway on Tuesday, two US officials told CNN, marking the highest number protected in a single operation during the war so far.

articles.title: ‘Habibi, come to Iran’: Tehran mocks Uncle Sam with Minesweeper game post over Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Middle East News: Iran’s embassy in Sierra Leone on Thursday challenged the US to “come to Iran” with an animated Minesweeper-style video set over the Strait of Hormuz..
articles.body: Iran’s embassy in Sierra Leone on Thursday challenged the US to “come to Iran” with an animated Minesweeper-style video set over the Strait of Hormuz.“Habibi (Uncle Sam), come to Iran!” the post read, referring to the US. The Iranian embassy paired the message with a 35-second animated video showing a 3D map of the Strait of Hormuz with a game of Minesweeper being played over it.The post came after US President Donald Trump said US forces had removed Iran-laid mines from the Strait of Hormuz and were continuing to move oil tankers through the key shipping route."We've controlled, and we are controlling the Hormuz Strait. We are bringing lots of boats out every day with millions of barrels of oil. We are, for the most part, doing it without trouble," Trump told reporters."They (Iran) were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and a mine drop. You know, we got rid of all the mines in the Hormuz Strait," he added.Fighting between the US and Iran has intensified this week after Washington struck Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, saying Tehran was planning to use them to lay mines in the waterway.In retaliation, Iran launched ballistic missiles at two US military targets in Jordan, claiming to have caused “heavy damage”. Jordan’s army, however, said it had intercepted eight missiles.US forces subsequently struck Iranian military targets in the second attack of the month, while Iran launched retaliatory strikes across the region despite a warning from Trump.According to US Central Command, the strikes targeted IRGC “air defense sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, mine laying capabilities, and communications sites”.Iranian state media, however, alleged that the US had struck a wedding. “We’re aware of the reports, which originated from Iranian state media. The U.S. military never targets civilians, unlike the IRGC,” Central Command spokesperson Timothy Hawkins said.The US-Iran war has now crossed the six-month mark, with Trump continuing to cite preventing Tehran from acquiring a nuclear weapon as his central objective.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.body: BENGALURU: A kitchen at Chairman’s Club in Sahakaranagar’s Dollars Colony was closed and seized after food safety officials found major hygiene and safety violations during a special inspection, the Karnataka Department of Food Safety and Drug Administration said on Friday.The inspection was conducted on September 3 by the department’s Food Safety Wing under the provisions of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, and related licensing and registration rules, following directions from Health and Family Welfare Minister U T Khader.Officials found and seized 40kg of expired chilli stored for use as a food product, the department said.The inspection also revealed improper labelling on 5kg of bread crumbs and 2kg of Sajeera food products, which did not comply with FSSAI regulations.Officials further found highly unhygienic conditions in food preparation and storage areas, alleged use or storage of unauthorised or prohibited artificial colours, and lapses in the handling and storage of food products.Vegetarian and non-vegetarian food items were also being stored together, in violation of prescribed food safety practices, according to the department.Expired food products were seized during the inspection. articles.body: Estonia’s defence minister Hanno Pevkur has resigned over an arms deal to supply artillery shells to Ukraine using €70 million in European Union funds and involving Indian company, Euronews reported.It emerged on Wednesday that Estonia had paid the amount upfront for the shells, but the Indian company Neco Defence Munitions involved had no previous record of selling artillery ammunition.The 2024 deal is now being challenged by Estonia in an arbitration case.Pevkur, who has been defence minister since 2022, said he was taking political responsibility for the controversy.“Although the minister does not count socks and ammunition or conduct contract negotiations, the National Audit Office’s criticisms, primarily concerning the activities of the Defence Forces and the Centre for Defence Investments, raise the question of political responsibility,” Pevkur said.The minister said he had not read the contracts, as defence ministers do not usually handle individual arms deals.“The defence minister does not conduct contract negotiations. articles.title: Texas ‘Killing Fields’: Man gets 20 years in teen’s death, first conviction tied to 4 women found at one site
articles.summary: US News: A Texas man has been sentenced to the maximum 20 years in prison over the death of 16-year-old Laura Miller, whose remains were among those found in a.
articles.body: A Texas man has been sentenced to the maximum 20 years in prison over the death of 16-year-old Laura Miller, whose remains were among those found in an area southeast of Houston where more than 30 girls and young women have turned up dead since the 1970s.The stretch around Interstate 45 became known as the “Texas Killing Fields” as bodies continued to be discovered over several decades and many of the deaths remained unsolved. James Dolphs Elmore Jr.'s conviction is the first linked to any of four women whose remains were found at one field off Calder Road in League City between 1984 and 1991.A Galveston County jury sentenced Elmore, 61, on Thursday, a day after finding him guilty of manslaughter in Miller's death. Prosecutors said he prepared cocaine that his longtime friend Clyde Hedrick administered to her.The Associated Press reported that Elmore approached Miller's father, Tim Miller, several years ago and told him he had been present when Laura died. The two men later met dozens of times.How did a decades-old case reach a jury?Elmore first contacted Tim Miller in 2022, nearly four decades after Laura disappeared. The two men met repeatedly, and Miller filmed some of their encounters, including visits to places linked to his daughter's death.Miller had spent years trying to find answers about Laura. After becoming frustrated with authorities during the search for his daughter, he founded Texas EquuSearch, a nonprofit that helps locate missing people.The Houston Chronicle reported that Miller paid Elmore about $33,000 over four years while seeking information that could help authorities build a case against Hedrick. Elmore also spoke to police about what he said happened on the night Laura died and said he had helped move her body to the Calder Road field.Prosecutors said Elmore prepared the cocaine and handed it to Hedrick, who administered it to Laura.Defence attorney Bill Agnew denied that Elmore was responsible and said his client likely would have been called to testify had Hedrick lived.“Clyde killed himself, and once that happened you've got one guy standing,” Agnew told jurors.Jurors deliberated for about an hour before finding Elmore guilty. The following day, they took roughly 30 minutes to impose the maximum 20-year sentence sought by prosecutors.During the trial, Tim Miller directly confronted Elmore over his role in Laura's death. “You handed it to Clyde Hedrick. You handed it,” Miller told him.Why did one field become central to the mystery?Laura disappeared in 1984. Her remains were found 17 months later, in 1986. Three other young women — Audrey Cook, Heidi Fye-Villareal and Donna Prudhomme — were also found at the Calder Road field between 1984 and 1991.The four deaths became part of the wider mystery associated with the Texas Killing Fields, a series of deaths and disappearances linked to the Interstate 45 corridor southeast of Houston.Elmore is the first person convicted in connection with any of the four Calder Road women. His conviction does not resolve who was responsible for the other three deaths.What happened to the man authorities had focused on?Authorities had also focused on Hedrick in connection with the four Calder Road deaths.In March, prosecutors said they planned to seek grand jury indictments against him over the deaths. Hedrick died by suicide before the cases could be presented.He had previously been convicted of manslaughter in 2014 in the death of Ellen Beason. Beason disappeared in 1984 and was found dead the following year. Hedrick was released on parole in 2022.Why do most ‘Texas Killing Fields’ deaths remain unsolved?Elmore's conviction is not the first involving the wider Texas Killing Fields cases. In 2022, Oklahoma death row inmate William Reece pleaded guilty in Texas to murdering Laura Smither, Jessica Cain and Kelli Cox. He received three life sentences.But most deaths associated with the Texas Killing Fields remain unsolved, and investigators believe more than one person may have been responsible.Kenneth Cusick, who was appointed Galveston County district attorney last year, has said his office would take a harder look at the cases.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith clear message to international students: The terms of studying in Canada are simple, earn your education and then …
articles.summary: Tech News News: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has reiterated that international students in Canada are expected to leave once their study visas expire if they have n.
articles.body: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has reiterated that international students in Canada are expected to leave once their study visas expire if they have not secured permanent residency. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Smith wrote, “A student visa is a temporary document to study in Canada. That was always understood. Our universities and colleges were built by Alberta taxpayers, first and foremost for Alberta students. Where there is room for international students, the terms are simple. Earn your education, then return home to build a life with it.”Her comments come against a backdrop of rising concern that some international students have been promised pathways to permanent residency that may not actually exist.The Portage College controversySmith's remarks were made in the context of protests by international students, many from India, who studied at Portage College and have since reported difficulties obtaining Post-Graduation Work Permits (PGWPs). While Smith rejected characterizing Portage College itself as a "diploma mill," she acknowledged that some programs may have overstated the immigration opportunities they offered students. She said there had been instances of unscrupulous operators setting up diploma-granting programs that took advantage of students. On the underlying policy, she was direct: if someone comes to Canada as an international student, their visa expires, and they don't have permanent residency, they need to go home.A tougher immigration environment nationallySmith's comments align with a broader tightening of Canada's immigration system. Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) has warned that working without proper authorization can carry serious consequences, including removal from Canada, a five-year ban on returning to the country, and a permanent fraud flag attached to an individual's immigration record. Unauthorized work can also negatively affect future visa applications and permanent residency prospects. IRCC has framed its recent reforms as an effort to protect students and strengthen the integrity of the international student program overall.What prospective students should knowIRCC has cautioned that admission to a Canadian college or university does not automatically translate into a work permit or a path to permanent residency. The agency advises students to independently verify their chosen institution, understand the specific eligibility requirements tied to their program, and remain cautious of anyone promising guaranteed immigration outcomes. More broadly, students are being urged to look beyond admission offers alone and carefully examine what their specific program actually permits them to do after graduation, rather than assuming a study visa will lead smoothly into long-term status in the country.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Meet 18-year-old Carter Grandbois who vibe coded his pricing calculator for 'junk collection', earns up to $15,000 a month, and wants to share the wealth too
articles.summary: Tech News News: Carter Grandbois was 16 when he started working for a junk-removal operator in Johnstown, Colorado, and noticed how much money he could make from rela.
articles.body: Carter Grandbois was 16 when he started working for a junk-removal operator in Johnstown, Colorado, and noticed how much money he could make from relatively small jobs. His boss kept a stack of cash in the centre console of his truck, and Grandbois went home and spoke to his father about starting their own operation. Within days, they had bought a trailer. Their first job brought in $500 for about 30 minutes of work.Now 18 and working full-time for himself, Grandbois says his business, Carter’s Junk Away, can bring in as much as $15,000 a month during peak season, a Fortune report noted. He said he eventually improved its profitability by building a pricing calculator, tracking job data and creating systems for generating leads. “I’m really into vibe-coding and creating software,” he explained. The calculator helped his crews bid jobs more consistently, allowing Grandbois to oversee more of the business without being on the truck.How Carter Grandbois used vibe coding to scale junk removalGrandbois said his junk-removal business initially struggled to become profitable consistently. The pricing calculator changed how his workers estimated jobs by giving them a system for calculating what to charge customers.“After that, we were able to be profitable on every single job,” he said. “When our team is out… they’re bidding jobs spot-on every single time. So every time they complete a job, I mean, we’re making anywhere from $50 to $200 without being on the truck.”Grandbois said he typically earns between $125 and $1,000 per junk-removal job. His employees are high school friends, while he increasingly handles parts of the operation from home rather than working on the truck himself.The software has also become something Grandbois wants to share with other people entering the industry. He has two calculators: a universal version and a “private junk-removal calculator,” which he described as being designed for a “more experienced junk-removal business.”Grandbois said he recognised that giving away the tools could potentially help competitors, but decided to share them anyway.He said, “I was like, ‘Hey, like everyone else could totally use this for their business.'”When asked about creating potential rivals by distributing his tools, he said: “That is one of the things with giving away stuff for free. You never know who’s watching the content. But at the end of the day, I know I’m doing something good for anyone else who’s trying to start.”His approach has been influenced partly by social media, where young entrepreneurs can watch other people build businesses rather than relying only on traditional business stories.Grandbois said, “It’s probably just like Instagram reels where you’re scrolling, and you’re like, ‘That guy has a Lamborghini. That dude has a McLaren. Why can’t I have one of those?'” His posts about his work on TikTok are under the account american.junkremoval.Carter Grandbois is building a business beyond junk removalJunk removal remains physical work, and Grandbois is building his company while he is 18. Unlike a traditional corporate job, the business does not provide employer-sponsored health insurance, a 401(k), or other employment benefits.Grandbois has also expanded beyond removing junk. He said he bought a lightly used Ford F-250 with about 10,000 miles and has started offering coaching to people interested in building junk-removal businesses.“We’ve started to do coaching to help other people who are interested in junk removal scale really quick,” he said.Grandbois estimated that junk coaching now accounts for about half of his business activity and said he has made roughly $40,000 from coaching this year. He said social media has also brought older prospective entrepreneurs to his content, including “a bunch of 40-year-old dads who are also interested in starting a business like this.”The business model is therefore changing from simply sending crews to collect unwanted items to selling the systems Grandbois developed while building the company. His pricing calculators, social-media content and coaching now sit alongside the original junk-removal operation.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.
